AN.title: ANSYS Hall
summary: ANSYS Hall is a four story, 36,000 square foot mixed-use building that incorporates a maker assembly space with immediate access to the outdoor Maker Courtyard, student collaboration space, classrooms and offices.

On the first floor of this building is TechSpark, which you can see into. This facility is a 16,000 square foot makerspace that provides resources, certification, classes and equipment for rapidly prototyping designs from ideas to reality for educational, extracurricular, and research activities. It is a hands-on learning and exploration space available to all current CMU students, faculty and staff. In addition to the highbay area for projects, the makerspace supports machining, wood working, embedded electronics, additive manufacturing, molding and casting with a dedicated wood shop, metal shop, professional shop with welding, hot metals room with jewelry making and metal casting, polymer casting room, computer lab with suite of engineering software, and a fabrication shop with 15 3D printers, 6 laser cutters and a sewing center.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Home of CMU's TechSpark macro-scale makerspace for the College of Engineering. Opened October 2019, 36,000 sq ft, four stories, designed by Bohlin Cywinski Jackson (the firm behind Apple's flagship stores and Pixar HQ) with CMU School of Architecture alumni Gregory Mottola and Kent Suhrbier leading. Funded by a naming gift from simulation-software company ANSYS, Inc. and LEED Gold certified in 2021. The signature feature is a glass high-bay with a literal garage door that rolls open onto the outdoor Maker Courtyard, letting students haul out solar-powered boats, Formula SAE racecars, and 20-foot steel bridges built by civil-engineering capstone teams. Upstairs, the ANSYS Simulation Lab overlooks the high bay, where undergrads model fluid dynamics and heat transfer using the same software sold to Boeing and Lockheed. The building anchors CMU's "Maker Ecosystem" — nano-scale fabrication in Scott Hall, component-scale in Hamerschlag, and macro-scale prototypes here. 18+ courses use the space each semester. Clubs like Carnegie Mellon Racing, the Robotics Club, and the Penguins-sponsored "Rethink the Rink" helmet-design team work here around the clock. No dining inside; Rothberg's Roasters in Scott Hall and La Prima in Gates are both a three-minute walk.

BH.title: Baker Hall
summary: Baker Hall is one of the oldest buildings on campus and connects to Porter Hall via a long, sloped hallway. Baker is home to the Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences. Our humanities are situated at the intersection of humanity and technology. For undergraduates, Dietrich houses 37 majors that are designed to be completed in 2 years, which allows students to add on additional majors, minors, and dual degrees. With this flexibility comes the ability to participate in experiences including internships, research, study abroad and more to prepare their students for the next step on their journey of graduate school or a career.
Next, we have **Baker Hall**, one of the oldest and most recognizable buildings on campus.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
Baker is the home of **Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences**. At CMU, we like to say our humanities sit right at the intersection of humanity and technology. Dietrich offers about 37 majors designed to be completed in just two years. This gives you huge flexibility to pick up a second major or a minor, or to spend time on internships and study abroad programs.

**Student Life Tip:**
Baker connects directly to Porter Hall via a very long, sloped hallway. It's a great indoor shortcut during Pittsburgh winters, but fair warning: the slope is deceptive. If you're rushing to class from the bottom of the hill, your calves will definitely feel the burn!
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Built in 1914 and 1919 as the original Administration Hall, Baker is the classroom-and-office anchor of the Marianna Brown Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences (renamed after a $265M gift in 2015). It houses English, History, Philosophy, Psychology, Social & Decision Sciences, Statistics & Data Science, and Pre-Law Advising. Designed by Henry Hornbostel's Palmer & Hornbostel firm, its signature feature is the long sloping main corridor that continues into Porter Hall with no stairs — designed so the building could be converted into a factory if Carnegie Tech failed as a university. Inside you'll find Guastavino tile vaulting, a signature spiral red-stone staircase, and a polished bronze bust of Andrew Carnegie. Giant Eagle Auditorium (BH A51) — named for the Pittsburgh grocery chain — is the big-lecture venue, and the Adamson Wing and Baker Cluster computer lab draw steady traffic. Dining is Ginger's Express on the lower level. The legendary student prank is "chairing" — riding an office chair down the sloped corridor, officially discouraged but culturally inescapable. The faculty legacy is remarkable: this was the administrative home of Herbert Simon (1978 Nobel in Economics, 1975 Turing Award), who helped found both CMU's Psychology Department and its School of Computer Science. Other Nobel laureates tied to Dietrich include Oliver Williamson (2009), Finn Kydland, and Edward Prescott (2004). CMU's cognitive psychology program ranks #5 nationally.

CFA.title: College of Fine Arts
summary: College of Fine Arts Building is an architectural creation of Henry Hornbostel, the college’s first dean, and is home to three of its five schools: architecture, art, and music. To speak a little more about each of these:
It includes the school of Music, Art, and Architecture
Here is the **College of Fine Arts building**, or simply **CFA**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This belongs to the **College of Fine Arts**. It serves as the creative headquarters for three of our five art schools: **Architecture, Art, and Music**.

**Fun Fact:**
This building is a masterpiece designed by Henry Hornbostel, who wasn't just the architect—he was also the college’s first dean! If you look up at the ceiling in the Great Hall inside, you'll see floor plans of famous historical buildings painted right onto the plaster. Hornbostel wanted architecture students to be able to study history just by looking up.

**Student Life Tip:**
The Great Hall is one of the most aesthetic spots on campus. If you sit there to study during the day, you’ll almost always get a free concert from the music students practicing in the nearby rehearsal rooms.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

The CFA building is Henry Hornbostel's 1912–1916 tribute to his own education at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, and it houses a college with a singular claim: CFA was the first U.S. institution to grant degrees in all five major art forms — Architecture, Art, Design, Drama, and Music. The cream-brick Beaux-Arts façade features five exterior niches with reliefs representing Medieval, Greek, Roman, Renaissance, and non-Western stylistic periods. A bust of Bacchus over the entrance is carved with Hornbostel's own face. The Great Hall's floors display inlaid marble plans of the world's great historical monuments so students literally walk over architectural history; canvas ceiling murals include Hornbostel's own Hell Gate Bridge in New York. Kresge Theatre (255 seats) is the recital and convocation venue; Alumni Concert Hall serves large ensembles. No dining inside, but Ginger's Express in Purnell and The Exchange in Posner are steps away. The alumni list is the tour-app headliner. School of Art: Andy Warhol (Pictorial Design, 1949), Philip Pearlstein, Mel Bochner, John Currin, Jonathan Borofsky. School of Drama (founded 1914, the oldest degree-granting drama program in the U.S., admit rate ~3%): Ted Danson, Holly Hunter, Ethan Hawke, Jeff Goldblum, Zachary Quinto, Patrick Wilson, Matt Bomer, Josh Gad, Josh Groban, Leslie Odom Jr., Billy Porter, Judith Light, Christian Borle, Rob Marshall, Steven Bochco. Music: Stephen Schwartz (composer of Wicked), Keith Lockhart (Boston Pops). Hornbostel himself wore red satin string ties, kept a pet monkey, and drove a convertible with his dog as co-pilot.

DH.title: Doherty Hall
summary: Doherty Hall contains some of the largest lecture style classrooms and renovated lab spaces for our Mellon College of Science students, in addition to lab and studio spaces for departments like Engineering, Chemistry, Biology and Art.

The Mellon College of Science houses 4 departments with 20 majors including biology, chemistry, physics, mathematics. Over 70% of undergraduates in this college do research. The college facilities also include a Cloud Lab that is the first academic Cloud Laboratory in the country and home to programmable robot-run experimentation instruments.

Also the new Richard King Mellon Hall of Sciences is coming in 2027 that will house our Mellon College of Science, the university's School of Computer Science and the public Institute for Contemporary Art. This mix of science, technology and art will spur exciting opportunities for cross-collaboration and embody Carnegie's Mellon spirit of innovation.
This massive building is **Doherty Hall**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
Doherty is the primary home for the **Mellon College of Science (MCS)**. Inside, you'll find everything from huge lecture halls to renovated labs for Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and Math. Uniquely, it also shares space with the School of Art and Engineering, meaning you might find a chemistry experiment happening right down the hall from a fine arts studio.

**Cool Feature:**
MCS is huge on innovation—over 70% of undergrads here do research! We even have the country’s first academic **Cloud Lab**, where students can program robots to run their experiments remotely. It's literally science fiction coming to life.

**Looking Ahead:**
While Doherty is historic, we are also looking to the future. In 2027, the new **Richard King Mellon Hall of Sciences** will open, bringing Science, Computer Science, and the Institute for Contemporary Art together under one roof to really supercharge that cross-collaboration.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Built in 1908 as the School of Applied Sciences, Doherty anchors Hornbostel's "Mall" and houses Mellon College of Science's Chemistry and Biological Sciences departments alongside College of Engineering's Chemical Engineering (continuously there since 1908). Named for trustee Henry L. Doherty. The Phase II addition (2009, LEED Silver) added three green roofs, including a semi-intensive roof with a bluestone-and-beach-pebble spiral walkway above C-level that doubles as an outdoor classroom. Doherty's defining quirk: no two floors have identical layouts, you cannot walk from the front of the first floor to the back without detouring, and the third and fourth floors exist only in two small towers that don't connect to each other. The maze continues into Wean Hall via five different stair/hallway connections — a rite of passage for every first-year trying to find class. Five large interdisciplinary teaching labs serve chemistry and chem-E students; 90% of chemistry majors do undergraduate research. No dining inside; La Prima in Gates or Stephanie's in the Mellon Institute are closest. Clarifying the original brief: the CMU Cloud Lab is not located in Doherty — it's in a CMU-owned building near Bakery Square — but Doherty chemistry faculty are its primary users. In December 2023, Assistant Professor Gabe Gomes published a Nature paper on "Coscientist," the first non-organic intelligent system to autonomously design and run a chemistry experiment, leveraging the Cloud Lab's 200+ instruments running 24/7. Doherty's role will shift when the $210M, 338,900-sq-ft Richard King Mellon Hall of Sciences opens in 2027 (groundbreaking April 12, 2024) as MCS's new primary home.

GHC.title: Gates and Hillman Centers
summary: Gates and Hillman Centers for Future-Generation Technologies are home to the School of Computer Science and Computational Biology Department. These Gold LEED Certified Centers were made possible by lead gifts from the Bill and Melinda Gates and the Henry L. Hillman foundations. The building also houses a Mission Control Center for the student project Iris Rover created by over 300 students from across the university that was the first of its kind to survive a launch and a zero-gravity environment.

The School of Computer Science was the first standalone school of Computer Science in the nation and launched the first Artificial Intelligence degree by a US University. The school houses five undergraduate majors including Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, Computational Biology, Human Computer Interaction, Robotics.
And here we have the stunning **Gates and Hillman Centers for Future-Generation Technologies**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This is the home of our world-renowned **School of Computer Science (SCS)**. CMU is a huge pioneer in this field—we established the nation's *first* standalone School of Computer Science and launched the first-ever undergraduate degree in AI. Students here study everything from Robotics and Human-Computer Interaction to Computational Biology.

**Student Project Spotlight:**
If you head inside, you can actually see a Mission Control Center for the **Iris Rover**. This project was built by over 300 students from across the university and holds the title of the first student project of its kind to survive a launch and zero-gravity environment. It’s a perfect example of how hands-on we get here.

**Fun Fact:**
The buildings were made possible by gifts from the Bill and Melinda Gates and Henry L. Hillman foundations. It’s not just high-tech on the inside; the building itself is Gold LEED Certified, meaning it's incredibly eco-friendly.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Completed in 2009 and dedicated September 22, 2009, GHC is the home of the School of Computer Science at 4902 Forbes Avenue. It's 217,000 sq ft across nine stories, designed by Mack Scogin Merrill Elam Architects, LEED Gold certified, built with a $20 million gift from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and $10 million from the Hillman Foundation. A cistern captures 500,000 gallons of rain and snowmelt per year for toilet flushing, and 98% of construction waste (19,000 tons) was diverted from landfill. The building won a 2012 AIA Institute Honor Award for Architecture, one of just nine worldwide that year. The signature feature is The Helix — a 650-foot-long spiral ramp connecting four stories inside the Gates atrium, famous for unofficial student stunts including mountain-bike descents and office-chair races. The black zinc diamond-shingle cladding is a modern reinterpretation of Hornbostel's brick; each of 310+ windows has its own silver zinc surround. The Randy Pausch Memorial Bridge to Purnell features 7,000+ programmable LED lights and symbolically links computer science to drama — Pausch taught both. Rashid Auditorium seats 250; its seats carry a cryptic binary pattern long rumored by students to be ASCII (analysts confirmed it's not). Other named spaces include the Luis von Ahn "Awesome Classroom" (gift of the Duolingo and reCAPTCHA founder, CS '03/'05), the Raj Reddy Conference Room, and the Moonshot Mission Control for lunar rover missions. Dining is Rohr Café on floor 3 — espresso, sandwiches, and a popular study spot with one of the healthier menus on campus. The Iris Rover launched January 8, 2024 aboard Astrobotic's Peregrine lander on the maiden flight of the Vulcan Centaur rocket. Built by 300+ students at just 4 pounds and shoebox-sized, Iris was billed as the first American, first university-developed, smallest, and lightest robotic lunar rover. Important accuracy note: the Peregrine lander suffered a propellant leak hours after launch and never reached the Moon, burning up over the Pacific on January 18, 2024 — but Iris successfully powered on and communicated from space, and a replica is displayed at the Smithsonian. Turing Award winners Raj Reddy, Manuel Blum, and Edmund M. Clarke are associated with the building, alongside pioneers Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, Randy Pausch ("The Last Lecture"), and former faculty member Geoffrey Hinton (2024 Nobel in Physics).

HBH.title: Hamburg Hall
summary: Here is **Hamburg Hall**, home to the **Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This college focuses on the intersection of people, policy, and technology. It uniquely houses both the School of Information Systems & Management and the School of Public Policy & Management under one roof.

**History & Architecture:**
Designed by Henry Hornbostel in 1915, this building was actually the U.S. Bureau of Mines before CMU acquired it. The recent renovation added the stunning **Teresa Heinz Rotunda** and a 'floating' classroom in the courtyard that is an architectural marvel.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Built 1915–1917 by Henry Hornbostel as the main building of the U.S. Bureau of Mines Central Experiment Station, Hamburg was acquired by CMU in 1984–1985 (U.S. Senator H. John Heinz III was instrumental) and is on the National Register of Historic Places since 1974. Today it's the headquarters of Heinz College — CMU's dual School of Public Policy & Management and School of Information Systems & Management. A 2013–2017, $18M+ renovation by GBBN Architects, funded by a $10M gift from The Heinz Endowments, inserted a 150-seat glass-enclosed auditorium into the former courtyard between Hamburg and Smith Halls, achieving LEED Gold for that phase. The Hamburg Hall 1000 rotunda was reimagined as a grand lobby, and a 3,600-sq-ft rooftop plaza sits above the new auditorium.

Heinz College has ~1,500 students and a branch campus in Adelaide, Australia. Weekly speakers have included Senator Bob Casey, former San Juan Mayor Carmen Yulín Cruz (MSPPM '86), Martin O'Malley, MoMA Director Glenn Lowry, and author Ijeoma Oluo. The school was renamed for Senator Heinz in 1992 following his 1991 death, with a lead gift from Teresa Heinz. Current Dean: Kristen Martin. Notable faculty include Alessandro Acquisti (privacy economics) and Jonathan Caulkins (drug policy). Alumna Leah Lizarondo founded Pittsburgh's 412 Food Rescue.

HH.title: Hamerschlag Hall
summary: Hamerschlag Hall is home to Electrical & Computer Engineering. The building's rotunda is one of the most iconic images on campus. This building also boasts a living roof
And here is the iconic **Hamerschlag Hall**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This building belongs to the **College of Engineering** and is the headquarters for the **Electrical & Computer Engineering (ECE)** department. It’s the heart of hardware and signals innovation on campus.

**Fun Fact:**
That rotunda at the end is one of the most famous images of CMU. It was actually designed to look like a spark plug to symbolize electrical engineering! Also, while you can't see it from down here, the building boasts a 'living roof' covered in plants to help manage rainwater and regulate temperature.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Hornbostel's 1912–1914 Machinery Hall — renamed in the 1960s for Arthur Arton Hamerschlag, first president of Carnegie Technical Schools — is home to the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering (450 undergrads, 300 grads) plus Mechanical Engineering labs and College of Engineering classrooms. The iconic feature is the domed round tower, a functional ~64-foot smokestack disguising the old power plant's flue and often called "the most beautiful smokestack ever created." Hornbostel designed the building as "the helm of an explorer's ship" pointing toward the Carnegie Institute, with a perfect axial view to Pitt's Cathedral of Learning. The entrance features a copy of the U.S.S. Pittsburgh cruiser's bow ornament. The cream-colored Kittanning brick was Hornbostel's deliberate signal of "practical, modern" identity versus red-brick Ivy League schools. Inside sits the HH-1107 Undergraduate Computer Cluster (recently upgraded as a makerspace), the Additive Manufacturing Lab, and the historic cleanroom facilities — though most nanofabrication has migrated to the 10,000-sq-ft Eden Hall Foundation Cleanroom in the adjacent Scott Hall (opened January 2016). In 2016, Volpatt Construction replaced 68 historic wood single-pane windows with custom-matched profiles. The tower is CMU's single most recognizable visual icon, appearing on nearly every postcard and promotional image. (Don't confuse Hamerschlag Hall with Hamerschlag House, a separate first-year residence nicknamed "Schlag" that was renovated in 2024–2025.)

HL.title: Hunt Library
summary: Here we have the unmistakable **Hunt Library**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This is the largest library on campus, housing four floors of collections specifically for the arts, humanities, and social sciences. It's also home to our University Archives and, uniquely, the **Hunt Institute for Botanical Documentation** on the fifth floor, which specializes in the history of plant science.

**Innovation Underground:**
Don't let the quiet upper floors fool you—the basement is buzzing with energy. It houses the **IDeATe** program, which stands for Integrative Design, Arts, and Technology. This is a collaborative hub offering nine minors where students merge tech and art—think Game Design, Animation, and Physical Computing. It’s a maker's paradise down there!
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Dedicated October 10, 1961, Hunt is CMU's main library and its only purpose-built library — the $2.8 million gift of Roy A. Hunt (an Alcoa founder, hence the aluminum-and-glass exterior) and his wife Rachel McMasters Miller Hunt, a legendary rare-book collector. Designed by Lawrie & Green, its cantilevered canopy names the donors on one side and the Rachel Hunt Botanical Library on the other, and nighttime LED illumination makes it glow from across The Cut. Five floors plus an A-level basement. The fifth-floor penthouse houses the Hunt Institute for Botanical Documentation — Rachel's personal rare-book legacy including medieval vellum manuscripts on medicinal herbs and Maria Sibylla Merian botanical books, "arguably the best collection of botanical books ever assembled by an individual in this country." The fourth floor has the Fine & Rare Book Room (600+ artists' books). The basement houses IDeATe — Integrative Design, Arts, and Technology — CMU's fabrication, media, physical computing, and soft technologies labs offering nine undergraduate minors fusing art and tech. The third floor is the dead-silent quiet floor, and the Hunt Library Gallery is currently hosting "Room to Imagine: 125 Years of Carnegie Mellon University" (Sept 11, 2025 – July 10, 2026), an immersive installation tracing CMU innovations from the iPhone interface to Toy Story, Duolingo, and Silly Putty. Dining is Maggie Murph Café on the first floor, operated since 2022 by De Fer Coffee & Tea, a specialty roastery founded by CMU alumnus Matt Marietti (MBA/TPR '10) and his wife Vanessa, roasting on-site daily. Extended hours run Mon–Fri 8 a.m. to 3 a.m., and during finals weekends extend to 3 a.m. as well — valid CMU ID required after 7 p.m.

MM.title: Margaret Morrison Carnegie Hall
summary: Margaret Morrison Carnegie Hall, affectionately known on campus as 'Maggie Mo'. This building originally housed the Margaret Morrison Carnegie College for Women, and it now houses some years of the design and architecture programs as well as our on campus children’s school!

The School of Design is an exploration of humanity and sustainable systems. With a focus on interdisciplinary learning, our programs prepare students for real-world design challenges by working collaboratively across fields. CMU was the first school to offer a degree in Industrial Design. Now it’s called “Product Design”.
You found **Margaret Morrison Carnegie Hall**, or as we affectionately call it, **'Maggie Mo'**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This building is part of the **College of Fine Arts** and currently houses the **School of Design**, parts of the School of Architecture, and even our on-campus Children’s School.

**History & Innovation:**
Originally, this was the Margaret Morrison Carnegie College for Women. Today, it carries on a legacy of innovation—CMU was actually the *first* school to offer a degree in Industrial Design (now called Product Design)! The focus here is on interdisciplinary learning and sustainable systems, preparing students to solve real-world problems.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Built 1906– 1907 by Henry Hornbostel as the Margaret Morrison Carnegie School for Women — CMU's original women's college, named for Andrew Carnegie's mother — this is now the home of the School of Design (CFA) plus parts of the School of Architecture, including the renowned Center for Building Performance and Diagnostics. Alumnae were called "Maggie Murphs." The women's college closed in 1973 due to declining enrollment as CMU fully integrated. The signature feature is the grand semicircular colonnaded rotunda with inscribed dedication from 1907 (you'll see references to both Ionic and Doric column orders across sources — the SAH Archipedia says Doric). Inside the rotunda, alumna Rebecca Deutsch ('04) installed stenciled quotes from women students across CMU history, responding to the original inscription. The rooftop hosts the Robert L. Preger Intelligent Workplace — a 7,000-sq-ft shimmering glass penthouse added in 1997 as an internationally recognized green-building research lab that predates LEED certification. A 1990–1996 Bohlin Cywinski Jackson renovation updated the interior. Hornbostel originally intended a matching rear wing with a second rotunda; it was never built. Notable alumna: Stephanie Kwolek (MMCC '46) — inventor of Kevlar.

PCA.title: Purnell Center for the Arts
summary: Purnell Center for the Arts is home to our School of Drama, the nation’s oldest degree-granting drama program, and includes state-of-the-art performance and education facilities like the Philip Chosky Theater and the Regina Gouger Miller Gallery. Whether you see yourself on stage, behind the scenes, or forging a creative path all on your own, our School of Drama’s specialized curriculum and dedicated, world-class faculty can help you get there with majors in acting/musical theater, design, dramaturgy, and production technology & management.
Next up is the **Purnell Center for the Arts**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This building houses the **School of Drama**, which is actually the nation’s *oldest* degree-granting drama program. It features incredible facilities like the Philip Chosky Theater and the Miller Gallery. Whether students are studying Acting, Musical Theater, or the technical wizardry of Production Management, this is where they hone their craft.

**Student Life Tip:**
You don't have to be a major to enjoy this building! I highly recommend catching a show at the Chosky Theater. The production quality is Broadway-level, and it’s a great way to see the stars of tomorrow before they get famous.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Opened in 2000 and named for alumnus-donor Verner S. Purnell, Purnell is home to the School of Drama — the oldest degree-granting drama program in the United States (founded 1914) — plus the Miller Institute for Contemporary Art. Approximately 110,000 sq ft, designed by Michael Dennis & Associates in a neoclassical style with a rotunda lobby mirroring Margaret Morrison's across campus. Admit rate for the drama program: around 3%, the lowest at CMU. Philip Chosky Theater is the 430–450-seat proscenium mainstage (convertible to thrust), featuring a 24′×18′ trap door section, tension grid, motorized orchestra pit, and computerized rigging — it replaced the 90-year-old Kresge Theatre. Helen Wayne Rauh Studio Theatre is the 130–140-seat flexible black-box. The building also houses the John Wells Video Studio (three-camera TV sound stage), a world-renowned lighting lab, and two dance studios. Miller ICA is a free, three-story, 8,000-sq-ft contemporary gallery founded in 2000 by alumna Regina Gouger Miller; it hosts the annual MFA Exhibition and BFA/BXA Senior Shows. The signature student tradition is "Playground: A Festival of Independent Student Work," launched in 2003 — the School of Drama cancels classes for a week while students produce 40–60+ original shows throughout the building. Notable Playground alumni include Josh Gad and Patina Miller. The alumni roll is legendary: Ted Danson, Holly Hunter, Zachary Quinto, Josh Groban, Patrick Wilson, Steven Bochco, Ethan Hawke, Sutton Foster, Megan Hilty, Cherry Jones, Judith Light, Rob Marshall, Billy Porter, Leslie Odom Jr., Renée Elise Goldsberry, Christian Borle. CMU alumni have won 66 Tony Awards, 99+ Emmys, and 13 Academy Awards, and CMU is the first and exclusive higher-education partner of the Tony Awards (since 2014), co-creating the Excellence in Theatre Education Award.

PH.title: Porter Hall
summary: Welcome to **Porter Hall**! This is actually the very first building ever constructed on our campus. It connects directly to Baker Hall and serves as a home for many of our interdisciplinary programs.

SH.title: Scaife Hall
summary: Alan Magee Scaife Hall of Engineering is a new 85,000 square-foot building comprising labs, a drone arena, offices, classrooms, and a café. The labs support research in a variety of subjects ranging from Biology to Robotics to Rapid Prototyping and are supported by 100 PhD workspaces directly adjacent to the lab spaces. The building is the home for the Mechanical Engineering Department.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Grand opening was November 9–10, 2023 for the new 85,000-sq-ft Scaife — double the size of the original 1962 building (the famous "Potato Chip" auditorium, demolished 2020). Named for benefactor Alan Magee Scaife. Designed by Philadelphia firm KieranTimberlake, with lead funding from the Allegheny Foundation. The building is the home of the Department of Mechanical Engineering and uses 25% less energy than the ASHRAE 90.1-2010 baseline, with 43% offset by CMU's off-site wind farm and a net pEUI of 77 kBtu/sf. The adjacent plaza was dedicated at opening as the Gordon E. Moore Engineering Quad, honoring the Intel co-founder.

The signature feature is a double-height high-bay drone/UAV arena whose floor is patterned specifically to aid motion-capture data capture — viewable from the circulation space above. Inside: 11 research labs across levels A and B (wet labs, dry labs, robotics, biosafety level 1, rapid prototyping, tissue culturing), about 100 PhD workspaces, 80+ offices, 19 meeting rooms, and a green rooftop garden connecting to ANSYS Hall's TechSpark via large operable doors. Public art installation "Making Way" by Jessica Stockholder was commissioned to match the building's "breaking boundaries" theme. Views from the Engineering Quad extend to Junction Hollow, Schenley Park, and Pitt's Cathedral of Learning. Dining is Redhawk Coffee on the first floor, opened fall 2023 with a September 28 grand opening. Redhawk is a Pittsburgh family-owned roastery; the CMU menu includes Driftwood Oven pastries, matcha lattes, mochas with Brunton's chocolate milk, and a signature honey-cinnamon latte. Fun fact: the original 1962 Scaife's state-of-the-art computer occupied the entire fourth floor, had to be carried in by helicopter, and had less processing power than a modern smartphone.

TCS.title: TCS Hall
summary: We arrived at the modern **Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) Hall**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
Opened in 2020, this building is a major hub for the **School of Computer Science**, specifically housing the **Institute for Software Research**. It is also home to the **MSCF** (Computational Finance) program. The interior is designed for connection, featuring a makerspace and open suites linked by 'communicating stairs' that you can actually see through the large windows.

**Industry Collaboration:**
The 5th floor is unique—it houses **TCS Paceport**, a dedicated space for academic collaboration between CMU and Tata Consultancy Services. It serves as a physical bridge between our research and the tech industry.

**Green Design:**
The building is Gold LEED Certified and features a beautiful rain garden and expansive courtyard outside, blending high-tech workspace with sustainable design.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Accuracy note: TCS Hall opened April 21, 2022 (not 2023), but it remains one of CMU's newest academic buildings. Dedicated in a ceremony with Governor Tom Wolf, Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran, and President Farnam Jahanian. Funded by a $35 million gift from Tata Consultancy Services in 2015 — at the time, the largest industry and international donation in CMU history — the gift also funds 17+ student fellowships and 20+ capstone projects. Roughly 90,000 sq ft on 5 stories above a ground-floor parking garage, LEED Gold certified, designed by Bohlin Cywinski Jackson (Gregory Mottola and Kent Suhrbier, both CMU architecture alumni). Located at 4615 Forbes Avenue, it's the first major building north of Forbes and serves as CMU's literal front door from Forbes Avenue. The building houses the Institute for Software Research (Software and Societal Systems, S3D) of the School of Computer Science, the Master of Science in Computational Finance (MSCF) program, the University Business Engagement Center, and TCS Pace Port Pittsburgh — TCS's fourth global co-innovation hub (5th floor, 8,000 sq ft), specializing in manufacturing and utilities innovation. Patterned brick, terracotta, and aluminum recall Hornbostel's historic palette in contemporary form. A two-story "Student Collaboration Porch" greets visitors; an outdoor "robot yard" and eco-sustainable rain garden sit alongside. Stephanie Dinkins' 44-foot mural "Good Thoughts, Good Words, Good Deeds" was installed in 2022. The flexible floor plates and drone high-bay make TCS the place where CS students, computational-finance quants, and engineering teams mix.

TEP.title: Tepper Quad
summary: Tepper Quad Building, is a 315,000 square foot state-of-the-art building, is home to the Tepper School of Business, the Coulter Welcome Center, fitness center, dining locations, JP Morgan and Chase AI Makerspace, and the Swartz Center for Entrepreneurship.

The Tepper School of Business houses three variations of undergraduate majors including Business administration major with 9 different concentrations, Multiple ways to earn an Economics major, and a Computational Finance major.

Here at CMU we do not have a central dining hall, but 30+ different eateries around campus. Inside the Tepper Building we have Rohr Commons featuring Build Pizza, Forbes Ave Subs, Tepper Taqueria, and Millie's Coffee ‘N Creamery.
Here is the massive and modern **Tepper Quad**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This 315,000-square-foot facility is home to the **Tepper School of Business**. It’s where students pursue degrees in Business Administration, Economics, and Computational Finance. But it's not just for business majors; it houses the **Swartz Center for Entrepreneurship** and the **JP Morgan Chase AI Makerspace**, proving that at CMU, business and technology always go hand in hand.

**Student Life Tip (Food Edition):**
One thing to know about CMU is that we don't have one giant central dining hall; instead, we have over 30 distinct eateries spread across campus. Tepper is a prime lunch spot—Rohr Commons inside has everything from custom pizzas and subs to a taqueria. And yes, there's a Millie's Coffee ‘N Creamery for your post-class caffeine or sugar fix!
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Opened September 13, 2018, the David A. Tepper Quadrangle is CMU's largest building at 315,000 sq ft across five stories — each floor is over an acre. Designed by Moore Ruble Yudell Architects (lead: Buzz Yudell) and built by PJ Dick for $201–205 million, funded in part by a $67 million lead gift from alumnus David A. Tepper (TPR '82) — billionaire hedge fund founder of Appaloosa Management and owner of the Carolina Panthers (NFL) and Charlotte FC (MLS). Additional lead gifts: $5M from David Coulter (TPR '71) for the welcome center and $31M from Jim Swartz (TPR '66, co-founder of Accel Partners) for the entrepreneurship center. The building is LEED Gold (73 of 79 points) with 82,000 sq ft of exterior glass giving 85% of the interior natural light, and uses the largest BubbleDeck plastic-air-bubble cement installation in North America to eliminate columns. A 120,000-gallon rainwater cistern serves building systems. Notable spaces: Simmons Auditorium (600 seats, CMU's largest and flat-floor reconfigurable), the Swartz Center for Entrepreneurship (15,000 sq ft with 10 startup "maker-space garages"), a 7,500-sq-ft fitness center, the JPMorgan Chase AI Maker Space, the Askwith Kenner Global Languages Room, and 24 tech-enabled classrooms. The Coulter Welcome Center is where every official CMU guided campus tour begins, led by Tartan Ambassadors 9 a.m.–4:30 p.m. daily (closed Wednesdays). Dining in Rohr Commons includes Tazza D'Oro (Pittsburgh-local coffee) and Pure (healthy bowls). In fall 2024, School of Design graduate students installed interactive updates including a miniature version of The Fence and a student-project wall. President Jahanian has called Tepper Quad CMU's "new front door to campus." A fun cultural aside: it's next door to the WQED studios where Mister Rogers' Neighborhood was filmed.

WEH.title: Wean Hall
summary: Here we are at **Wean Hall**, instantly recognizable by its concrete, brutalist architecture.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This is a major hub for the sciences and engineering. It houses **Mathematical Sciences, Physics, Material Science**, and some undergraduate **Computer Science** spaces. It’s also home to the **Engineering and Science Library**—if you look at the exterior, those unique sloped panes of glass are actually the windows for the library!

**Campus Topography Fun Fact:**
Welcome to CMU's unique geography: we are standing at the main entrance right now, but we are actually on the **5th floor**! The building extends down into the ravine for a total of eight floors. Also, if you head down to the 4th floor, there's a skyway bridge that connects you directly to Newell-Simon Hall.

**Student Life Tip:**
If you need a serious caffeine fix, Wean is home to **La Prima Espresso**. It’s a local Pittsburgh coffee roaster, and many students swear it is hands-down the best coffee on campus.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Opened 1971, renamed October 9, 1981 for industrialist Raymond "Jack" Wean (Carnegie Tech 1917), designed by Dahlen K. Ritchey for $15.5 million (1971 dollars). Wean is CMU's sole brutalist building — a massive reinforced-concrete bunker 8 stories tall, built into the side of a ravine so that only 3 stories plus a mechanical penthouse are visible from the Mall side, the remaining 5 descending into the hillside. No two floors have identical layouts. Nicknamed "The Turtle." It was Pittsburgh's largest all-concrete building after Three Rivers Stadium was imploded in 2001. Houses the Department of Mathematical Sciences, parts of the School of Computer Science (classrooms, labs, clusters), Physics labs, the Sorrells Engineering and Science Library, and Machine Learning Department offices on the subterranean level. Wean connects to Doherty through a warren of stairs and hallways at five different levels — the site of the student game "Capture the Flag with Stuff." Major facade repairs in 2013–2014 exposed and encased rusted rebar ahead of the SCS 50th anniversary. A recent lobby renovation by IKM Architecture added a glass "crystal" prism under the brutalist overhang to create a light-filled, recruitment-friendly entrance housing an expanded La Prima Espresso. Dining is La Prima Espresso Company — a staple for 30+ years, Pittsburgh's only certified organic coffee roaster, serving Italian-style espresso, nitro cold brew, Mediterra Bakehouse pastries, and curried chickpea wraps. Fun fact: students claim an unofficial world record for "most bottle caps stuck in holes in a building" — plastic bottle caps are the exact size of the form-tie holes in Wean's concrete walls. Scott Fahlman, whose office sat in the CS computing ecosystem, invented the :-) emoticon at CMU in 1982. The Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center (founded 1986 by CMU physicist Michael Levine) is closely affiliated with Wean's computing history.

CYH.title: Cyert Hall
summary: Next is **Cyert Hall**, located right near the entrance to campus.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This building is the nerve center for campus technology, housing **Computing Services** and the Office of the CIO. It’s also the home of the **Office of International Education (OIE)**, so if you are studying abroad or are an international student, you'll likely visit here.

**History & Innovation:**
It is named after **Richard Cyert**, CMU's sixth president. He was a visionary who launched the 'Andrew' computing network, which was the first to link all computers on campus together. Fittingly, this building was originally known as the University Computing Center.

**Student Life Tip:**
Need a quiet place to work or have a tech issue? Cyert has a computer cluster on the lower level that is often less crowded than the library. Plus, the IT Help Desk is located here if your laptop ever decides to quit on you during finals week!
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

president Originally the University Computing Center, renamed for Richard Michael Cyert (1921–1998), CMU's 6th president from 1972–1990 and co-author of the seminal 1959 A Behavioral Theory of the Firm. Cyert's presidency transformed CMU "from an Eastern technical school to a premier American university," launching the largest expansion in school history and focusing the university on computing. The building is a workmanlike concrete mid/late-20th-century academic structure at 5000 Forbes Avenue. It houses CMU Computing Services — the university's main network infrastructure and ITS data center (rack-mount colocation, web servers, AFS/DFS/NFS storage, authentication systems); the Office of International Education (Suite 101 — study abroad advising, F-1/J-1 visas, I-20/DS-2019 issuance); the Osher Lifelong Learning Institute (in a 2021 renovation of 5,730 sq ft by NEXT Architecture); Desk Services tech help (Room 119); and student computer labs. The CS Department itself was established in 1965 with a $5M Mellon grant — Alan Perlis (the very first ACM Turing Award recipient in 1966) was its first head. Cyert Hall is effectively the plumbing of CMU's digital life — the first stop for international students handling visas and for students launching study-abroad journeys.

WH.title: Warner Hall
summary: Warner Hall is home to the Office of Undergraduate Admission on the second floor. Their office is open from 8:30AM - 4:30PM Monday through Friday if you would like to stop in for a walk-in appointment.
The HUB and Enrollment Services also reside here, which would be where you get your Student ID if you choose to attend CMU.
And here we have **Warner Hall**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This building is the administrative heart of your enrollment journey. It houses **The HUB**, which handles enrollment services. Most importantly for future Tartans, this is the very spot where you will come to pick up your official Student ID card on your first day!

**Visitor Tip:**
The **Office of Undergraduate Admission** is located right here on the second floor. They are open Monday through Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. If you have any burning questions that I can't answer today, feel free to head up there for a walk-in appointment after the tour.
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Opened 1965–1966 and named for John Christian Warner, CMU's 4th president (1950–1965), Warner is CMU's main administrative building and sits at 5000 Forbes Avenue — the official mailing address for most of the campus. It houses the Office of the President (currently Farnam Jahanian, CMU's 10th president), the Office of Undergraduate Admission (2nd floor, walk-in M–F 8:30–4:30), the HUB on the lower level (CMU's one-stop enrollment center for financial aid, student accounts, registrar, and ID cards), and most senior administrative offices. A recent Landau Building Company renovation updated 42,011 sq ft across all six stories in under 8 months, bringing restrooms to ADA compliance and fully upgrading HVAC. The quiet treasure inside is the George Nakashima furniture collection — 60 pieces of master-craftsman Nakashima furniture commissioned 1965–1966 by interior designer Paul Planert for Warner's opening, gifted by the Scaife family. Iconic pieces including the Conoid Bench are still in active use in the President's and Admissions offices; it's one of the largest institutional Nakashima collections in the world and is featured on the Bloomberg Connects app. Every prospective student passes through: self-guided tour maps are available in the first-floor vestibules at both Warner and the Coulter Welcome Center, and enrolling students return to The HUB to pick up their CMU Student ID card. Out front on the lawn sits the iconic 80-foot Walking to the Sky sculpture by Jonathan Borofsky (2006, donated by trustee Jill Gansman Kraus) — a canonical campus photo spot. Fun techie detail: CMU's DNS LOC record geographically points to Warner Hall, making it the "official" location of cmu.edu on the internet.

CUC.title: Cohon University Center
summary: Jared L. Cohon University Center is our student union. Here students can take advantage of the student fitness facilities, catch a show at the black-box theater, visit the chapel, gather with other students in meeting rooms, or get lunch in one of many eateries.

You see our Scotty statue mascot that was funded and created by multiple CMU alumni. Our mascot is the Scottish Highland Terrier or Scottie for short. We like to call the dog “Scotty” who is a confident, independent and spirited breed. We students like to rub its nose for goodluck, so feel free to try that out before leaving this stop!

Additionally, located in this building is The Center for Student Diversity and Inclusion. The Center offers resources to enhance an inclusive and transformative student experience for our student population that joins us from 120 different countries. The Center is focused on access, success, campus climate and intergroup dialogue.
Here is the **Jared L. Cohon University Center**, or as we call it, the **CUC**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This is our student union, so it doesn't belong to just one college—it’s for everyone. It's the hub of campus life where you'll find our fitness facilities, a black-box theater, a chapel, and plenty of eateries to grab lunch.

**Community Spotlight:**
Inside, you'll also find the **Center for Student Diversity and Inclusion**. They offer resources and support for our diverse student body, which represents over 120 different countries!

**Fun Fact & Tradition:**
See that statue of the Scottish Highland Terrier? That’s 'Scotty,' our mascot! It was actually funded and created by CMU alumni. It’s a huge campus tradition to rub his nose for good luck, so definitely give it a try before we head to the next stop!
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

The Jared L. Cohon University Center is CMU's 24/7 student union, named in 2014 for 8th president Jared L. Cohon (1997–2013). Original building opened 1996 (Michael Dennis & Associates, postmodern echo of Hornbostel's Beaux-Arts); the 62,000-sq-ft expansion by CannonDesign with LGA Partners opened May 2016, winning the MBA Building Excellence Award for New Construction. The new Lee Lobby features floor-to-ceiling windows, two native-plant rain gardens, and the signature art piece: Dale Chihuly's "Frank-Ratchye End of the Day Chandelier," a massive multi-colored blown-glass sculpture donated in 2013 by trustee Edward H. Frank and Sarah Ratchye to honor President Cohon, its colors symbolizing his commitment to diversity. Key spaces: McConomy Auditorium (445 seats, stadium-style), Rangos Ballroom (holds 450, dividable into three, hosts the Activities FAIR), Wiegand Gym, Maureen B. Cohon Cardio Fitness Center (10,000 sq ft), a 25-yard, 8-lane Olympic-sized swimming pool with diving well, squash/racquetball courts, a Studio Theater black-box, a 24-hour multi-denominational prayer room, University Store, Art Store, and Tech Store. Dining is one of CMU's deepest lineups: Schatz Dining Room (campus's only all-you-care-to-eat buffet, 2nd floor), Au Bon Pain at Skibo Café, El Gallo de Oro (Mexican), Revolution Noodle (build-your-own Malatang noodle bowls, bao buns, bubble tea; opened 2022), Tazza D'Oro espresso, and Entropy+ convenience store. The Tartan Express food truck parks outside in Legacy Plaza. Outside in Merson Courtyard sits the bronze Scotty statue — CMU's Scottish terrier mascot — unveiled April 8, 2022 during Spring Carnival, sculpted by alumnus Ray Kaskey (CFA) and funded by CFA alumna Kathy Sabec Dax and her late husband Robert Dax. The tradition is to rub Scotty's nose for good luck. The Scottish terrier became CMU's official mascot in 2007. The CUC hosts The FAIR (350+ student organizations), Late Night at CMU, orientation, and Spring Carnival events.

POS.title: Posner Hall
summary: Posner Hall is adjacent to the Hall of the Arts, which is home to some teaching and rehearsal spaces for the School of Music. This building is home to a student-favorite eatery called The Exchange as well as the Student Academic Success Center. The  Student Academic Success Center focuses on creating spaces for students to engage in their coursework and approach to learning through options like academic coaching, subject-specific tutoring, effective communication strategies, accommodations for students with disabilities, and language support for multilingual learners.
Next stop is **Posner Hall**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:** Situated right next to the Hall of the Arts, Posner Hall acts as a central support hub for students from all colleges. It is home to the **Student Academic Success Center**, a vital resource where you can find subject-specific tutoring, academic coaching, communication workshops, and accommodations for students with disabilities.

**Student Life:** Ask any student about Posner, and they will likely mention **The Exchange**. It’s a fast-casual eatery located inside that is a huge student favorite—definitely a go-to spot for grabbing a quick lunch!
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Built 1990–1993 as an expansion of the Graduate School of Industrial Administration by Kallmann McKinnell & Wood, Posner Hall was the original home of the Tepper School of Business until Tepper relocated to Tepper Quad in 2018. A full 2021 GBBN renovation (LEED Gold) repurposed the building for the Student Academic Success Center (1st floor), registrar classrooms, Dietrich College departments, and the Institute for Politics and Strategy. A gift of Henry Posner Jr. and his family. The star attraction is Kraus Campo (2005) — a rooftop garden-as-sculpture designed by conceptual artist Mel Bochner (CFA '62) — who died February 12, 2025 at 84 — with landscape architect Michael Van Valkenburgh, commissioned by trustee Jill Gansman Kraus (A'74). Features include a central platform covered in a distinctive numerical pattern reflecting Bochner's interest in mathematical order, winding orange pathways through plantings, and a 6-foot-by-58-foot tiled quotation — words referencing physicist Arthur Eddington on the second law of thermodynamics, attributed in context to Ludwig Wittgenstein, transcribed in reverse order as a literal visual puzzle that students walk past daily without ever quite finishing. Dining is The Exchange on the first floor — a 20-year CMU institution serving custom deli sandwiches (student favorite: "The Leonardo"), made-from-scratch soups, hot entrées, a salad bar, and La Prima coffee, sourced from local BreadWorks and Turner's Dairy Farm. The adjacent earth-sheltered Posner Center (2004, 11,400 sq ft) houses the Posner Memorial Collection of rare books and early calculating machines. In March 2025, the Posner Foundation committed $8 million to CMU Libraries Special Collections, funding a Perkins Eastman-designed renovation of the Posner Center scheduled to conclude fall 2025, reimagining it as "part museum, part laboratory for the humanities."

HWC.title: Highmark Center for Health, Wellness and Athletics
summary: The Highmark Center is a 160,000 square foot building recently opened which unifies robust health services, contemporary facilities and educational programs that support students’ minds, bodies and spirits in a comprehensive care model. It includes new full-service clinical areas as an expanded University Health Services; private and supportive spaces for Counseling and Psychological Services; and a modern athletics facility for practice, performance, training and athlete care.
Here is the **Highmark Center for Health, Wellness and Athletics**.

**Purpose & Affiliation:**
This state-of-the-art facility is a university-wide resource, meaning it belongs to *everyone*. It serves as a unified home for your mind, body, and spirit, housing University Health Services, Counseling and Psychological Services (CaPS), and our varsity and intramural athletics all under one roof.

**Fun Facts:**
Even though it's brand new (opened in 2024), it preserves our history by being built around the foundation of the old Skibo Gym. Also, take a look at the floor tiles in the lobby—they are designed to mimic the rhythm of a human heartbeat!
Additional tour-guide research (cross-verified against CMU sources):

Accuracy correction: the Highmark Center's cost is $105 million, not $200M+, per all official CMU sources. Groundbreaking was November 19, 2021; the building opened August 2024 for fall semester, with an official dedication October 24, 2024. 160,000 sq ft (142,000 new + 16,000 renovated) across four stories. Designed by Bohlin Cywinski Jackson, built in 36 months by Mascaro Construction, pursuing LEED Gold. The $35 million lead gift from Highmark, Inc. (Fall 2019) was one of the largest corporate partnerships in CMU history. Donor-named spaces include the Buncher Suite for Wellness, the Hoplamazian Family Well-Being Lab, the Rohr Intercollegiate Golf Training Facility, and the Block-Kelley Tartan Room. The building replaces the historic Skibo Gymnasium (1924), which hosted CMU's first basketball game (Feb. 5, 1924 vs. Pitt) and a Louis Armstrong performance. Skibo's core was preserved and woven into the new Center — its original exterior wall now lives inside as the secondary gym wall, 6,000 sq ft of salvaged wooden flooring appears in the Tartan Hall of Fame, the varsity weight room displays the original center-court Tartan logo, and copper feature walls are made from the patina-aged copper roofs of the old North Gym and Thistle Hall. Signature spaces: Main Arena (16,000 sq ft, seats ~1,000, home to varsity basketball and volleyball), secondary recreational gym (with six hoops, volleyball, three badminton courts, pickleball), Turf Fieldhouse inside Skibo's preserved shell (turf, running lanes, batting cages), Rohr Intercollegiate Golf Training Facility (three virtual training screens — used by the 2024 NCAA D-III Champion women's golf team), athletic training suite, student-athlete lounge. Upstairs: UHS clinic on the 3rd floor (with a juice bar), and CaPS counseling on the 4th floor with a Wellness Garden. The Buncher Suite includes four contemplation nooks, two ablution rooms, a gallery, and a circular Interfaith Room. UHS Wellness To Go vending machines provide on-site access to emergency contraception, sexual-health supplies, and OTC medications. Art includes Guadalupe Maravilla's Descansa Espíritus/Rest Spirits — six polished aluminum hammocks suspended as a symmetrical mobile, installed October 2024. Dining is Shake Smart — protein shakes, fruit smoothies, and açaí bowls. The Center is the first CMU facility to integrate physical health, mental health, spiritual life, and athletics under one roof, a model CMU positions as a national leader in holistic student wellness. It sits right next to Schenley Park.

WTS.title: Walking to the Sky
summary: Walking to the Sky is a 100-foot-tall stainless steel sculpture by artist Jonathan Borofsky, installed on CMU's campus in 2006. Standing at a striking 75-degree angle, it features a procession of figures climbing toward the sky, led by an elder and followed by people of all ages, races, and walks of life.

The piece is meant to celebrate the human spirit of optimism, discovery, and self-discovery — a fitting symbol for a university built on curiosity. Located on the lawn near the College of Fine Arts and Forbes Avenue, it's one of the most photographed spots on campus.

FENCE.title: The Fence
summary: The Fence is one of CMU's most beloved traditions and is widely considered the most painted object in the world. Originally a wooden footbridge railing built in 1916, it has been continuously painted by student groups for over a century to advertise events, celebrate milestones, and share messages with the community.

Tradition dictates that the Fence can only be painted between midnight and sunrise, by hand using a brush, and a group must be present to guard it 24/7 in order to keep it. By 1993, layers of paint had grown so heavy that the original Fence collapsed under its own weight; the current concrete and steel structure was built to carry the legacy forward.
